title: Working Scientifically
seo_title: Year 10 Science: Working Scientifically Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_code: AC9S10I01, AC9S10I02, AC9S10I03, AC9S10I04, AC9S10I05, AC9S10I06, AC9S10I07, AC9S10I08
standard_text: Develop investigable and research questions and testable hypotheses; plan safe, ethical investigations with risk assessments; analyse primary and secondary data including gradients, correlations and uncertainty; evaluate methods, claims and sources; and communicate evidence-based conclusions (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Year 10 science inquiry content descriptions).
meta_desc: Free Year 10 science worksheets on working scientifically: research questions, hypotheses, risk assessments, gradients, correlation and cause, uncertainty, evaluating methods and claims. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Analyse trends with gradients and correlations, and evaluate the method before trusting the conclusion.
body_html:
How to think about it

Senior science depends on careful analysis and honest evaluation.

  • Plan: a research question, a testable hypothesis, variables and a risk assessment with controls for each hazard.
  • Analyse: gradient = rise ÷ run (with units); describe correlations by direction and strength; report uncertainty.
  • Evaluate: sample size, controls, bias, sources of error and whether a correlation could have another cause.
Example

Line through (2, 6) and (6, 18). Gradient?

rise 18 − 6 = 12

run 6 − 2 = 4

12 ÷ 4

Answer: 3

Example

Ice-cream sales and sunburn both rise. Cause?

both rise in sunny weather

Answer: correlation, not cause

Common mistakes

  • Treating a correlation as proof of cause.
  • Calculating a gradient as run ÷ rise.
  • Judging a method by whether the results matched the prediction rather than by its design.

faq.q: How do I calculate the gradient of a graph?
faq.a: Choose two points far apart on the line of best fit. Gradient = (change in y) ÷ (change in x), with units of y-units per x-unit.
A table that lists each hazard in an investigation, the risk it causes and the control used to reduce it, such as safety glasses for acids.

faq.q: How do I evaluate an investigation?
faq.a: Check whether variables were controlled, samples were large enough, measurements were precise and accurate, and whether the conclusion goes beyond the evidence.

items.q: What is a research question?
c: a focused question that can be answered by collecting and analysing data
items.e: Example: How does temperature affect the rate of enzyme activity?

items.q: In a risk assessment for heating a liquid with a Bunsen burner, which is the best control?
c: stay on firm ground and work with a partner
wear safety glasses and wipe up spills
use a heatproof mat, tongs and tie hair back
cut away from your body on a board
items.e: The hazard is burns from hot glassware or flame.

items.q: What is the purpose of a risk assessment?
c: to identify hazards and plan controls before an investigation
items.e: It keeps everyone safe.

items.q: What makes data reliable?
c: repeated measurements that give similar results
items.e: Repeatability builds confidence.

items.q: In a risk assessment for observing the Sun, which is the best control?
c: stay on firm ground and work with a partner
use a heatproof mat, tongs and tie hair back
use a sand tray and keep feet clear
never look directly at the Sun; use a pinhole projector
items.e: The hazard is eye damage.

items.q: Liam uses a motion sensor instead of a stopwatch to measure a falling ball. How does this change the uncertainty?
c: It removes the need to repeat.
It reduces the uncertainty in the time measurements.
items.e: Better equipment improves precision.

items.q: In a risk assessment for dropping masses from a height, which is the best control?
c: wear safety glasses and wipe up spills
never look directly at the Sun; use a pinhole projector
use low voltage and switch off before changing wires
use a sand tray and keep feet clear
items.e: The hazard is masses falling on feet.

items.q: In a risk assessment for heating a liquid with a Bunsen burner, what is the main hazard?
c: slipping or falling into the water
burns from hot glassware or flame
items.e: A risk assessment lists each hazard and how to control it.

items.q: A group times a ball rolling down a ramp once for each height. Which change would best improve the investigation?
c: Control light, water and soil for both groups.
Survey a random sample from many schools.
Repeat each height several times and find the mean.
items.e: One trial per height is not reliable; random errors are not reduced.

items.q: Jack measures bubbles from pondweed at 10, 20, 30 and 40 cm from a lamp. Which variable must he control?
items.e: A lamp also heats the water; use a heat screen.

items.q: A student measures the temperature of water by reading the thermometer from above at an angle. Which change would best improve the investigation?
c: Read the scale at eye level.
Survey a random sample from many schools.
Use a large, independent, blind trial with a control group.
items.e: Parallax error can make every reading wrong.

items.q: In a risk assessment for connecting a circuit to a power pack, which is the best control?
c: use low voltage and switch off before changing wires
seal the plates and do not open them after incubation
use a sand tray and keep feet clear
use a heatproof mat, tongs and tie hair back
items.e: The hazard is electric shock or hot wires.

items.q: In a risk assessment for connecting a circuit to a power pack, what is the main hazard?
c: slipping or falling into the water
items.e: A risk assessment lists each hazard and how to control it.

items.q: Zara's experiment did not support her hypothesis. What should she write?
c: that the data did not support it, with possible reasons and improvements
that the hypothesis was proven anyway
items.e: Science reports results honestly.

items.q: What does peer review do?
c: experts check research for errors before it is published
items.e: It increases trust in findings.

items.q: In a risk assessment for culturing bacteria on agar plates, what is the main hazard?
c: slipping or falling into the water
items.e: A risk assessment lists each hazard and how to control it.

items.q: What is accuracy?
c: how close a measurement is to the true value
how close repeats are to each other
items.e: Precision is how close repeats are.

items.q: Noah wants to know whether a creek is polluted. Which is the best method?
c: sample water at several sites over several weeks and test it
test one cup of water once
ask people if the creek looks dirty
items.e: More samples give more reliable conclusions.

items.q: In a risk assessment for using dilute hydrochloric acid, which is the best control?
c: use a heatproof mat, tongs and tie hair back
never look directly at the Sun; use a pinhole projector
wear safety glasses and wipe up spills
use low voltage and switch off before changing wires
items.e: The hazard is acid splashing in the eyes.

items.q: A group reports that bean plants grew 5.23847 cm. What is the main problem with this method?
c: There were too many controlled variables.
The result has more decimal places than the ruler can measure.
The results should be changed to match the prediction.
items.e: Record to the precision of the ruler, such as 5.2 cm.

items.q: A group repeated a test of the temperature rise of 100 mL of water heated for 1 minute four times: 13.5 °C, 14.0 °C, 14.5 °C, 14.0 °C. What is the range of the results?
items.e: Range = largest − smallest = 14.5 − 13.5 = 1.0 °C.

items.q: In an experiment, the number of yeast cells changed from 250 to 300. What is the percentage increase?
items.e: Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100 = 50 ÷ 250 × 100 = 20%.

items.q: Why do CSIRO and BoM scientists use data from many weather stations?
c: to reduce the effect of errors at any one station and show true trends
items.e: Large data sets give more reliable conclusions.

items.q: A friend says rain always comes after his footy team wins, because it happened twice. What is the main problem with this claim?
c: Two events are not enough data, and there is no reason one causes the other.
The claim is wrong because the scientists were young.
The claim is proven because it was published online.
Nothing is wrong; one result is enough.
items.e: Good evidence needs a fair test, a large sample, a control and no bias.

Nothing is wrong; one result is enough.
The claim is wrong because the scientists were young.

items.e: Good evidence needs a fair test, a large sample, a control and no bias.

items.e: Enzymes denature at high temperatures.

items.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary data?
c: Primary data you collect yourself; secondary data comes from other sources.
items.e: Both can be used to support a conclusion.

items.q: Why is a correlation not enough to prove that one variable causes another?
c: A third factor might cause both, or the link could be chance.
items.e: Controlled experiments test cause.
